question: Compare memory bandwidth of the Apple M4 Pro and M5 Pro.
raw_answer: The Apple M4 Pro has a memory bandwidth of 273 GB/s [1], while the Apple M5 Pro has a memory bandwidth of 307.2 GB/s [4]. Therefore, the M5 Pro has higher memory bandwidth than the M4 Pro.

Its Apple M4 Pro (20 Core) graphics unit has twice as many cores. The higher memory bandwidth of 273 GB/s on the M4 Pro compared to 120 GB/s on the M4 significantly improves gaming performance. The Apple M-series is known for high energy efficiency. The Apple M4 delivers strong performance with low power consumption.

The**Apple M4 Pro (14-CPU 20-GPU)** consumes more energy under load but remains very efficient for its performance class.
The **Apple M4** offers very good value for money for the average user. The more expensive **Apple M4 Pro (14-CPU 20-GPU)** justifies its price with significantly higher multi-core and graphics performance.

passages.heading: Super cores and performance cores
passages.text:
## Super cores and performance cores

Both M5 Pro and M5 Max use the identical CPU split: 18 cores made up of 6 “super cores” and 12 performance cores. Apple uses “super core” as a label across its 2026 chip family, including M6, but has not published a technical definition distinguishing a super core from a performance core beyond the naming itself.

Where the two chips diverge is the GPU and memory ceiling. M5 Max’s GPU scales to 40 cores against M5 Pro’s 20, and its memory ceiling doubles, from 64GB to 128GB, with bandwidth nearly doubling too, from 307GB/s to 614GB/s. Both chips share a 16-core Neural Engine.

passages.heading: M4: an AI-focused engine with wider deployment
passages.text:
### M4: an AI-focused engine with wider deployment

**M4 (2024)** debuted unusually in iPad Pro before moving to Mac. It paired a faster CPU and next-generation GPU with a Neural Engine designed for the on-device machine-learning era. M4 Pro and M4 Max increased CPU, GPU, memory bandwidth, and Thunderbolt capability for Mac mini and MacBook Pro. For many buyers, the key M4 change was not a single AI feature but a better balance of sustained performance and efficiency across small desktops and notebooks.

passages.heading: M5: graphics, neural accelerators, and the high-end split
passages.text:
### M5: graphics, neural accelerators, and the high-end split

**M5 (2025)** pushed more AI capability into the GPU architecture, while the 2026 M5 Pro and M5 Max expanded the family for demanding professional workflows. Apple's strategy became less numerically tidy at the top: **M5 Ultra**, announced in August 2026, paired a 36-core CPU with up to an 80-core GPU, supported up to 512GB of unified memory, and reached up to 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth. It launched beside M6 rather than waiting for every product to share the same generation number.

passages.heading: Base, Pro, Max, and Ultra: what the suffixes mean
passages.text:
### Base, Pro, Max, and Ultra: what the suffixes mean

**Base M-series** chips prioritize efficiency and mainstream performance for MacBook Air, entry MacBook Pro, iMac, and Mac mini. **Pro** adds CPU and GPU resources, memory bandwidth, external-display support, and ports for heavier development, audio, photography, and video work. **Max** pushes GPU capability and memory capacity further for 3D, effects, high-resolution video, and large local models. **Ultra** is the workstation tier, joining multiple high-end dies for Mac Studio-class workloads.

A newer base chip can beat an older high-end chip in some single-core, media, or AI tasks while losing badly in sustained multicore work, GPU rendering, memory capacity, or display support. Compare the workload and the entire Mac, not just the “M” number.

passages.heading: Apple M5 Pro (18-CPU 20-GPU)
passages.text:
The LPDDR5X-9600 unified memory is offered with up to 64 GB and is connected via a much wider memory interface than on the M5. CPU, GPU and Neural Engine access the same data directly, which speeds up large projects and AI models.

All in all, the M5 Pro with 18 CPU and 20 GPU cores is a very fast yet efficient chip for professional notebooks. If you mainly need more graphics performance, the M5 Max offers an even stronger GPU, but for most professionals the M5 Pro is the more balanced choice.

Geekbench 4, Geekbench 5, and Geekbench 6 benchmark averages for all Apple Silicon MacBook Pro models are listed below (2020-Current).

EveryMac.com diligently has hand compiled -- and independently averaged -- these Geekbench benchmarks from aggregate user results submitted to Primate Labs for each Apple Silicon MacBook Pro. This data is unique to the EveryMac.com website.

Generally, EveryMac.com has calculated averages within a few weeks of the release of each new Mac. Via a combination of our own custom algorithm for automated analysis and manual human review, benchmark results that are significant outliers, inaccurately tagged, not running the macOS, or otherwise errant are omitted prior to calculating an average. For many models, EveryMac.com runs Geekbench software directly on one or more devices, too.

On Apple Silicon MacBook Pro models, Geekbench 4 is running under Rosetta 2 with a single CPU core and all CPU cores. Geekbench 5 and Geekbench 6 provide native performance with a single CPU core and all CPU cores.  **Higher numbers are better. Geekbench benchmarks cannot be compared across versions.**

Geekbench benchmarks also are provided on EveryMac.com's specs pages for all Apple Silicon MacBook Pro models and within the Ultimate Mac Comparison feature.
